claim.addressed_criterion: A read account explicitly relates worldly-information safety for modal knowledge to the truth of the same earlier utterance under a changed assessment context and its retraction obligation.
claim.confidence_scope: Partial engagement is established in read texts; no accessible source located that derives assessment-sensitive retrospective retraction from worldly-information safety. Access gaps and incomplete reference indexing prevent a literature-wide absence or novelty claim.
claim.coverage: The original bibliography contains 53 works from 1967–2024, only four from 2020 onward and none after 2024. The prior 26 available PDFs cover 1996–2024, with most dated 1996–2021; three are from 2020 onward. The October 28, 2026 sweep searched 2018–2026 literature on contextualism, relativism, expressivism, dynamic semantics, epistemic contradictions, probability operators, retraction and assessment sensitivity. Across the initial sweep and focused L3 followup, 44 modern candidates were recorded and 25 exact full texts obtained, plus three previously missing originals; 54 PDFs are now local in total (26 pre-existing and 28 additions). Coverage includes recent surveys, formal models, empirical tests and responses, but 19 selected modern works and 24 originals remain unavailable to this client (43 operator requests). Older foundational chapters, complete books, the strongest 2024 safety/expressivism comparisons and recent empirical reviews remain material access gaps. This is a ranked, bounded search of indexes and public sources, not an exhaustive review. A failed search or inaccessible paper does not establish an open problem or novelty. The old lack-of-model/test claim is addressed; the other two flagged problems are partially addressed. Acquired files have not been extracted into the frozen ARA evidence: existing route verdicts and generated arguments therefore retain their original evidential limits. The focused L3 verdict is partial: Beddor–Goldstein already engages retraction and assessor information, and Dinges (2021) explains retraction through estimates of epistemic qualities, including safety. The accessible texts do not establish a derivation of MacFarlane’s assessment-sensitive retraction obligation from worldly-information safety. The two strongest Hawke (2024) comparisons remain inaccessible; no novelty claim follows.
claim.partial_basis: Mighty Knowledge itself combines a retraction motivation, assessor-based rejection, a worldly-information safety semantics, and an optional assessor-credence interpretation. Dinges2021 directly links safety-type estimates with retraction behavior while rejecting the need for relativism. Neither supplies the exact requested integration.

search_scope.notes: Bounded ranked search pages: broad OpenAlex75 and Crossref40 per query; supplementary queries100 each. One book-cursor request refused401; nine legitimate publication-year filters recovered all449 indexed citing records. API matches were screened for relevance; biomedical retractions/safety and title collisions excluded. Metadata screening is not full-text reading of every cited work.
